Baltic Darij 1

GeometryTrianglesCircles
Game: Move the corners of a triangle and watch four marked points sit on one circle.
How to play: Drag A, B or C, or focus a corner and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show more lines and marks, and press Check the claim to test what you see.
Look for the math

Drop a perpendicular from B and from C onto the bisector at A. Join the altitude foot and the midpoint of BC to those two points. The four points you get always sit on one circle, however you drag the triangle. That is the surprise this applet shows.

Four points, one circle

Call the feet from B and C onto the angle bisector at A by P and Q. Let Ha be the foot of the altitude from A, and A' the midpoint of BC. The claim is that P, Q, A' and Ha are concyclic. The logic test measures the distance from each point to the centre of the circle through the other three on the opening triangle, on six fixed triangles and on 1,500 random ones; the four distances agree to within about 1 part in 10 billion.

A line through the middle

Reflect B across the bisector at A. Its reflection R lies on the line AC, and the bisector cuts BR exactly in half: P is the midpoint of BR. In triangle BCR, the segment from the midpoint of BR to A' (the midpoint of BC) is a midline, so it is parallel to the base: A'P || AC. The same argument from the other side gives A'Q || AB. Since the bisector makes equal angles with AB and AC, these two parallel segments are equally long: A'P = A'Q. All three statements hold at every triangle in the test; tick lines to see the full lines and the point R.

A circle with diameter AC

Both angles AHaC and AQC are right angles, so Ha and Q lie on the circle whose diameter is AC (Thales' theorem). Tick big circle to see it. This puts Ha and Q on a second circle, and comparing angles on the two circles is what proves the first claim.

Angles that match

The applet's solution compares two angles that are sometimes equal and sometimes supplementary; directed angles modulo 180° make one argument cover both cases. The upshot is angle(A'P, A'Ha) = angle(QP, QHa), which is exactly the test for four concyclic points. A bonus: triangle QPHa is inversely similar to ABC, with QPHa = ABC and PQHa = ACB. The test checks all three angle pairs, the three side ratios and the reflected orientation too. Nothing on the page turned out to be false.

Try a very flat triangle with Ha outside BC: the circle still passes through all four points, and the two "equal" angles become supplementary instead of equal.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
